document.title: The Budget Statement and Economic Policy of the Government of Ghana for the 2026 Financial Year

topics.title: Front matter
topics.plain_summary: This part of the document is front matter (cover, contents, or lists) rather than policy itself.

topics.title: 2026 Budget Presentation and Statutory Reports
topics.plain_summary: The government presented the 2026 Budget Statement and Economic Policy, along with required annual reports on petroleum funds and the African Union Import Levy, for parliamentary approval.
topics.why_it_matters: This budget sets the financial and economic rules for the entire country for the year, dictating how public funds are managed and which sectors receive government attention.
key_changes: The Budget Statement and Economic Policy of Government for the year ending 31st December 2026 was moved for parliamentary approval.

topics.title: New Bills, Regulations, and Economic Policy Proposals
topics.plain_summary: The government is introducing several new bills and policy requests, including the repeal of the COVID-19 Health Recovery Levy, changes to value-added and health insurance taxes, and the implementation of an AI-powered trade data system.
topics.why_it_matters: Proposed tax adjustments and levies directly change what everyday citizens pay for goods, education, health services, and how government money is spent.
key_changes: The Value for Money Bill
The Virtual Asset Service Providers Bill
The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Bill
The COVID-19 Health Recovery Levy (Repeal) Bill
The Ghana Education Trust Fund (GETFund) (Amendment) Bill
The National Health Insurance (Amendment) Bill
The Public Procurement Regulations
Request for approval for a Revised Investment Policy of the Ghana Petroleum Funds
Request for approval to implement an AI-powered trade data analytics system to support customs revenue mobilization.

topics.title: 2026 Wages and Economic Dialogue
topics.plain_summary: The National Minimum Wage and Base Pay for 2026 have been agreed upon in partnership with Organized Labour and employers, establishing the National Tripartite Committee as a permanent forum for economic dialogue.
topics.why_it_matters: Workers and employers are directly impacted by agreed wage adjustments, ensuring predictability and stability in incomes and labour relations for the year.
key_changes: Together with Government, we have successfully agreed on the National Minimum Wage and Base Pay for 2026, ahead of this Budget...

topics.title: Strategic Priorities for Growth, Jobs, and Transformation
topics.plain_summary: The government outlined three main priorities for 2026: stabilizing the macroeconomy, accelerating job creation through infrastructure and agriculture, and strengthening security and social sectors like education and health.
topics.why_it_matters: Focusing on job creation, infrastructure, education, and health directly improves daily living conditions, public services, and economic opportunities for ordinary citizens.
key_changes: Consolidating Macroeconomic Stability
Accelerating Economic Transformation and Job Creation
Strengthening Security and Social Sectors for Inclusive Growth

topics.title: Global Economic Developments and Inflation Outlook
topics.plain_summary: Global economic growth is expected to stay modest at 3.2 percent in 2025 and 3.1 percent in 2026. Across the world, inflation is gradually slowing down due to better supply chains and tighter monetary policies. In Sub-Saharan Africa, average inflation is projected to drop from 13.1 percent in 2025 to 10.9 percent in 2026, though everyday people may still face challenges from food price changes and climate shocks.
topics.why_it_matters: When global inflation and commodity prices change, it directly affects the cost of imported goods, food prices, and the cost of living for ordinary citizens. A drop in regional inflation means price increases could start slowing down, giving households some relief on everyday expenses.
key_changes: Headline inflation is projected to decline from 4.2 percent in 2025 to 3.7 percent in 2026.
In Sub-Saharan Africa, average inflation is forecast to ease from 13.1 percent in 2025 to 10.9 percent in 2026.

topics.title: Commodity Market Trends and Prices
topics.plain_summary: Global commodity prices are seeing mixed trends. Crude oil and gold prices are shifting, while cocoa prices spiked due to poor weather and lower production in West Africa, though prices are expected to stabilize as supply improves.
topics.why_it_matters: Changes in global commodity prices directly impact farmers who grow cash crops like cocoa, as well as businesses and consumers who rely on fuel and imported goods tied to global oil prices.
key_changes: Brent crude oil prices are expected to average US$68 per barrel in 2025, down from US$79 in 2024.
Cocoa prices have surged to an average of US$7,800 per metric tonne in 2025, up from US$5,900 in 2024, due to adverse weather and production shortfalls in West Africa.

topics.title: Ghana's Progress Toward ECOWAS Convergence
topics.plain_summary: Ghana has made strong improvements in meeting regional economic goals, successfully hitting five out of six ECOWAS convergence criteria by late 2025. This includes keeping the budget deficit low, maintaining healthy foreign reserves, stopping central bank budget financing, stabilizing public debt, and seeing a stable exchange rate.
topics.why_it_matters: Meeting these regional financial targets shows that the national economy is stabilizing. For the average person, a stable exchange rate, controlled public debt, and zero central bank borrowing help protect the value of money and support a more predictable economic environment.
key_changes: In 2025, the fiscal deficit is projected at 2.8 percent of GDP, below the 3 percent benchmark;
Gross external reserves now cover 4.8 months of imports, exceeding the minimum threshold of three months;
Central Bank financing of the budget remains at zero, compared to the regional ceiling of 10 percent of previous year’s revenue;

sections.title: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025
sections.heading: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Macroeconomic Performance and Economic Growth
topics.plain_summary: Ghana's economy grew strongly in the first half of 2025, driven mainly by the services and agriculture sectors. Inflation dropped sharply, bringing price relief to ordinary households and businesses.
topics.why_it_matters: The drop in inflation and the lowering of borrowing costs make everyday goods more affordable and make it easier for businesses and ordinary people to access credit. This economic recovery helps restore purchasing power and improves the standard of living for everyday families.
key_changes: Overall GDP expanded by 6.3 percent in the first half of 2025, up from 5.1 percent during the same period in 2024.
Inflation fell from 23.8 percent in December 2024 to 8 percent in October 2025, returning Ghana to single-digit inflation.
The Bank of Ghana reduced the monetary policy rate from 28 percent to 21.5 percent.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Fiscal Performance and Public Debt Reduction
topics.plain_summary: The government achieved a major turnaround in public finances by cutting wasteful spending, increasing tax compliance, and reducing the country's public debt ratio.
topics.why_it_matters: Lower public debt and disciplined government spending free up money for vital social programs, schools, and hospitals instead of paying heavy interest on debt. This fiscal responsibility brings greater stability to the economy.
key_changes: Public debt to GDP ratio reduced from 68.9 percent at the end of September 2024 to 45.0 percent a year later.
The primary balance on a commitment basis improved from a deficit of 3.0 percent of GDP in 2024 to a surplus of 1.6 percent by September 2025.
Short-term interest rates fell sharply, with the 91-day Treasury-bill rate declining from about 29 percent to around 10.6 percent.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Energy Sector and COCOBOD Reforms
topics.plain_summary: The government renegotiated costly power contracts and reformed the cocoa sector to clear debts, protect farmer incomes, and ensure a stable supply of electricity.
topics.why_it_matters: Higher cocoa prices directly reward farmers for their hard work and protect their incomes. Meanwhile, reforms in the power sector prevent massive government debts from accumulating, leading to a reliable electricity supply for homes and businesses.
key_changes: Successfully renegotiated Power Purchase Agreements with Independent Power Producers, saving the nation over US$250 million.
Set the producer price of cocoa at GH¢58,000 per tonne for the 2025/26 crop season.
Rationalized cocoa roads contracts from GH¢21 billion to GH¢6 billion.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Exchange Rate and External Sector Improvements
topics.plain_summary: Ghana's currency strengthened significantly against major foreign currencies due to higher export earnings from gold and cocoa, alongside strict management of imports.
topics.why_it_matters: A stronger Cedi lowers the cost of imported goods, reduces fuel price inflation, and makes it cheaper for the country to pay its foreign debts. This helps stabilize market prices for everyday shoppers.
key_changes: The Ghana Cedi appreciated by 34.6 percent against the US Dollar, 28.0 percent against the British Pound, and 20.5 percent against the Euro as of November 2025.
Gross international reserves rose to approximately US$11.4 billion, providing about 4.8 months of import cover.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Administration Sector and Office of Government Machinery
topics.plain_summary: The Administration Sector focuses on strengthening democratic institutions, public financial management, and decentralisation. The Office of Government Machinery manages strategic leadership, state protocol, investor relations through the GIPC, enterprise support via MASLOC, and higher education access through the Scholarship Secretariat.
topics.why_it_matters: Ordinary citizens benefit from enhanced government accountability, improved access to local and international education funding, business growth support for small enterprises, and more efficient public services designed to reduce bureaucratic hurdles.
key_changes: In 2026, the Secretariat will scale up human capital development, with a renewed focus on science, technology, and ICT education as key enablers of innovation and competitiveness.
In 2026, the Secretariat will broaden scholarship coverage to include emerging fields like digital innovation, climate science, and biotechnology...
In 2026, the Public Sector Reform Secretariat will operationalise the National Public Sector Reform Strategy II (NPSRS II)...

topics.title: Civil Service, Parliament, Audit Service, and Public Services
topics.plain_summary: The structure of Government was streamlined into 23 Ministries. Parliament passed 27 bills and implemented new Standing Orders. The Audit Service recovered misappropriated public funds and tackled payroll fraud, while the Public Services Commission advanced the roll-out of the Human Resource Management Information System (HRMIS).
topics.why_it_matters: These changes improve the efficiency, integrity, and transparency of government operations. Removing ghost names from payrolls and auditing public funds protects taxpayer money and ensures public resources are directed toward meaningful national development.
key_changes: In 2026, the Office will embark on a review of the Civil Service Act, 1993 (PNDCL 327) and the Civil Service Regulations, 1960...
In 2026, the Commission will complete the rollout of the HRMIS to all MDAs and MMDAs, conduct a comprehensive Human Resource Audit across government institutions...
In 2026, the Audit Service will scale up its audit operations by conducting comprehensive financial, compliance, and performance audits across all MDAs, MMDAs, and State-Owned Enterprises.

topics.title: Foreign Affairs, Finance, and Ghana Gold Board
topics.plain_summary: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs improved passport services and rolled out chip-embedded biometric passports. The Ministry of Finance strengthened fiscal discipline, pushed debt strategies, and managed climate finance projects. The Ghana Gold Board spearheaded gold value chain reforms, achieving record small-scale gold exports and supporting reserve accumulation.
topics.why_it_matters: Citizens benefit from secure, internationally compliant travel documents, better-regulated economic policies, and enhanced financial stability. Small-scale gold miners operate under clear, formalized frameworks that boost national economic growth and foreign exchange reserves.
key_changes: A major breakthrough came with the rollout of chip-embedded biometric passports on 28th April 2025...
Looking ahead, 2026 will mark the rollout of the Ministry’s Strategic Transition from Renting to Infrastructure Development (STRIDE) initiative...
Beginning in 2026, it will roll out a comprehensive Gold Traceability System, ensuring every gram of gold purchased can be traced...

topics.title: Local Government, Media, and Planning Commissions
topics.plain_summary: The Ministry of Local Government advanced decentralisation, local economic development, social safety nets, and urban spatial planning. The National Media Commission, National Development Planning Commission, and Right to Information Commission worked to enforce regulatory compliance, media responsibility, long-term development planning, and citizens' access to public information.
topics.why_it_matters: Communities experience better local governance, improved infrastructure, and cleaner environments. Citizens gain easier access to public information through newly opened regional RTI offices, strengthening their ability to participate in national democracy.
key_changes: In 2026, the 10th Cycle of DPAT will introduce a new performance tracker to align MMDCEs’ performance indicators...
In 2026, the Commission will operationalise Regional Complaints Settlement Offices to decentralise complaint handling...
In 2026, the RTIC will open five new regional offices in Cape Coast, Ho, Takoradi, Koforidua, and Tamale.

topics.title: Agriculture, Fisheries, and Lands Management
topics.plain_summary: Agriculture serves as the economic anchor through the Feed Ghana Programme, vegetable development, and irrigation projects. The Ministry of Fisheries upgraded biosecurity, passed new acts, and targeted aquaculture growth. The Ministry of Lands improved land registration through digital systems, promoted reforestation, and intensified anti-illegal mining operations.
topics.why_it_matters: Farmers and fishermen receive crucial inputs, technical training, and better storage facilities, which lower food price volatility and secure livelihoods. Landowners benefit from automated registration systems that reduce litigation, while strict enforcement against illegal mining protects water bodies and the environment.
key_changes: In 2026 we will supply 4,388 mt of maize seed, 31,000 mt of rice seed, 240 mt of sorghum seed, 2,791 mt of soybean seed, and 272,000 mt of fertilisers...
In 2026, Government will introduce new Regulations to guide vessel licensing, aquaculture operations, surveillance, and post-harvest practices...
In 2026, we will revise the National Land Policy and Lands Commission Act, and finalise the Legislative Instrument for the Land Act...

topics.title: Trade, Industry, Tourism, Environment, and Energy
topics.plain_summary: The Ministry of Trade drove industrialization through the Ghana FIRST framework and the Accelerated Export Development Programme. Tourism focused on heritage preservation. Environmental policies introduced green financing and carbon management. Energy initiatives expanded electricity access, explored petroleum and nuclear power, and promoted clean cooking and e-mobility.
topics.why_it_matters: Local businesses and exporters gain expanded market access across Africa, boosting job creation. Consumers benefit from a reliable energy supply, affordable electricity tariffs, clean cooking solutions, and environmental protections that combat climate change.
key_changes: In 2026, Government will complete the review of the AfCFTA National Policy Framework and support at least 200 MSMEs to access new markets...
In 2026, the Authority will issue about 80 new licenses in 2026 and intensify international investment promotion.
In 2026, large-scale distribution [of LPG cookstoves] will begin nationwide.

topics.title: Infrastructure Sector: Roads, Railways, Housing, Water, and Transport
topics.plain_summary: Infrastructure investments connected communities and industries through road construction, railway rehabilitation, affordable housing projects, water and sanitation system upgrades, and digital and mass transport enhancements.
topics.why_it_matters: Improved roads, rail networks, and mass transport systems reduce travel times and shipping costs for goods. Citizens gain better access to safe drinking water, affordable housing schemes, sanitation facilities, and reliable digital connectivity.
key_changes: The 2026 programme targets maintenance of an additional 25,000 kilometres [of roads], alongside completion of all major ongoing highway projects.
A total of 8,000 units are expected to be made habitable under the first phase [of Saglemi Affordable Housing] in 2026.
In 2026, work will continue on the Sekondi-Takoradi and Sunyani Water Supply Projects, targeting an additional 1.2 million beneficiaries.

topics.title: Social Sector: Education, Labour, Sports, Youth, Health, and Social Protection
topics.plain_summary: The Social Sector enhanced basic and tertiary education, teacher welfare, and TVET training. It maintained industrial peace, expanded sports development, promoted youth empowerment, advanced universal health coverage with hospital rehabilitations, and enforced social protection laws for vulnerable groups.
topics.why_it_matters: Students receive a modernized, skills-focused education alongside expanded healthcare access through new hospitals and fee policies. Workers enjoy industrial harmony, while vulnerable citizens and victims of trafficking receive structured social protection and welfare support.
key_changes: In 2026, Government will overhaul the basic school curriculum from kindergarten to primary six to equip learners with practical skills...
In 2026, the [Scholarship/Education] programme will be extended to Senior High Schools nationwide [for sanitary pads distribution].
In 2026, Government will continue rebuilding La General Hospital, establish six regional hospitals, expand CHPS compounds, and modernise medical equipment nationwide.

topics.title: Public Safety Sector: Justice, Defence, Law Enforcement, and Anti-Corruption
topics.plain_summary: The Public Safety Sector focused on protecting citizens, fighting crime, and upholding the rule of law. The Attorney-General handled prosecutions and legal drafting, EOCO and the OSP recovered misappropriated public funds, the military secured borders, and police and immigration services maintained internal security and border control.
topics.why_it_matters: Effective law enforcement, reduced court backlogs, and aggressive anti-corruption investigations protect public finances and ensure a secure environment. Vulnerable individuals receive free legal aid to access justice fairly.
key_changes: In 2026, the Ministry [of Justice] will defend about 400 civil suits, review 100 agreements and contracts, and prosecute at least 1,700 criminal cases...
In 2026, EOCO will investigate about 450 cases, prosecute over 20, and recover an estimated GH¢250 million.
In 2026, CHRAJ will conduct corruption risk assessments for the Lands Commission and the Ministry of Roads and Highways.

sections.title: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS
sections.heading: SECTION 5: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS

topics.title: 2026 Macroeconomic and Fiscal Targets
topics.plain_summary: The government has established macroeconomic targets for 2026 and the medium-term to maintain economic stability, control inflation, and support sustainable growth. For 2026, the overall real GDP growth is targeted at at least 4.8 percent, end-year inflation is expected to reach 8.0 percent, and a primary surplus of 1.5 percent of GDP is set on a commitment basis. Total revenue and grants are projected at GH¢268.1 billion, while total expenditure on a commitment basis is programmed at GH¢302.5 billion (or an appropriation total of GH¢357,105,639,079.87). Public servants will receive a 9 percent negotiated increase in base pay under the Single Spine Salary Structure.
topics.why_it_matters: These targets and fiscal allocations directly influence the cost of living, employment opportunities, and public service delivery for average citizens. Controlling inflation at 8 percent helps protect household purchasing power, while structured government spending aims to fund infrastructure, education, health, and social protection programs that directly benefit communities.
key_changes: Overall real GDP growth of at least 4.8 percent
End-year inflation of 8.0 percent
A primary surplus of 1.5 percent of GDP on commitment basis
Total Revenue and Grants projected at GH¢268.1 billion
Total Expenditure programmed at GH¢302.5 billion on commitment basis
Total appropriation of GH¢357,105,639,079.87 for the fiscal year ending 31st December 2026

source_references.section: SECTION 5: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS

topics.title: Growth Drivers and Sector Investments
topics.plain_summary: The government is rolling out targeted policies to stimulate private sector growth, exports, and human capital development. Key initiatives include the Big Push infrastructure program focusing on roads, the Feed Ghana Programme supported by Farmers’ Service Centres and Farm Banks, the Free Secondary Education Programme, the National Apprenticeship Programme, and the National Employment Trust. Additional digital initiatives involve the One Million Coders Programme and a FinTech Growth Fund.
topics.why_it_matters: These growth drivers create direct opportunities for employment, skills training, and business expansion. Farmers gain better access to inputs and markets through new facilities, youth benefit from expanded digital and vocational training programs, and business owners experience improved physical infrastructure that eases trade and lowers operational costs.
key_changes: Implementation of the Big Push Programme focusing on road infrastructure for 2025 and 2026
Rollout of a five-year Trade Sector Support Programme
Expansion of the Free Secondary Education Programme and National Apprenticeship Programme
Launch of the Feed Ghana Programme through Farmers’ Service Centres and Farm Banks

source_references.section: SECTION 5: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS

topics.title: Petroleum Revenue Projections and Allocation
topics.plain_summary: Projected petroleum receipts for 2026 are estimated at US$985.50 million, based on a benchmark crude oil price of US$76.22 per barrel and total crude oil output of 37.95 million barrels. Out of the benchmark revenue after transfers to the national oil company, US$556.6 million is allocated to the Annual Budget Funding Amount, while US$238.6 million goes to the Ghana Petroleum Funds.
topics.why_it_matters: Petroleum revenues directly contribute to the national budget and fund public infrastructure and services that impact the entire population, while a portion is safely saved in petroleum funds for future generations.
key_changes: Benchmark crude oil price set at US$76.22 per barrel
Benchmark crude oil output estimated at 37.95 million barrels
Total projected petroleum receipts of US$985.50 million
Allocation of US$556.6 million to the Annual Budget Funding Amount and US$238.6 million to the Ghana Petroleum Funds

source_references.section: SECTION 5: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS

topics.title: Medium-Term Debt Management Strategy
topics.plain_summary: The government is implementing a debt management strategy for 2025–2028 to keep public borrowing sustainable and cost-effective. The strategy involves resuming benchmark bond issuances in 2026, utilizing concessional financing from multilateral partners, and enforcing strict debt limits such as capping Treasury bills and keeping short-term debt low.
topics.why_it_matters: Disciplined debt management lowers the country's debt-servicing burden, freeing up public funds to invest in essential services like health, education, and infrastructure rather than paying off high interest loans.
key_changes: Resuming benchmark bond issuance in 2026
Limiting debt maturing within one year to 15±5 percent of total debt
Capping Treasury bills at 20±5 percent of domestic debt
Restricting USD-denominated debt to no more than 70 percent of external debt

source_references.section: SECTION 5: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS

sections.title: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES
sections.heading: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: Comprehensive Value Added Tax (VAT) Reforms
topics.plain_summary: The government is modernising the VAT system to make it fairer, simpler, and more business-friendly. These changes reduce the effective VAT rate, eliminate specific levies and taxes on mineral prospecting, raise the threshold for small businesses, and leverage digital tools for collection.
topics.why_it_matters: For the average person and business owner, these changes reduce the cost of doing business and put more money directly into people's pockets—an estimated GH¢5.7 billion total for households and businesses in 2026. Raising the VAT registration threshold relieves small and micro enterprises from the heavy burden of collecting and administering VAT, while removing the COVID-19 levy lowers costs on everyday goods and services.
key_changes: abolish the COVID-19 Health Recovery Levy
reduce the effective VAT rate from 21.9% to 20%
raise the VAT registration threshold from GH¢200,000 to GH¢750,000
abolish VAT on reconnaissance and prospecting of minerals

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: Establishment of the Value for Money Office (VfMO)
topics.plain_summary: An independent statutory body is being established to review, certify, and sanction public contracts before money is spent. This office acts as a permanent guardian to prevent inflation of project costs, budget overruns, and waste.
topics.why_it_matters: This change ensures that public funds are not lost to inflated prices or abandoned projects. For the average citizen, it means public infrastructure like roads, schools, and hospitals are delivered at fair prices and higher quality, saving billions of cedis and rebuilding trust in how public money is spent.
key_changes: Establishing an independent statutory VfMO with legal power to review, certify, and sanction.
A mandatory VfM Certificate will be a condition for contract award, payment, or continuation.

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: Agricultural Initiatives: Oil Palm Policy, Equipment, and Local Food Sourcing
topics.plain_summary: The government is rolling out major agricultural interventions including a multi-year oil palm development policy with a $500 million finance window, the distribution of agricultural machinery through Farmer Service Centres, and a directive forcing schools to buy local food supplies.
topics.why_it_matters: These programs directly support local food producers, poultry farmers, and smallholders by guaranteeing a ready market in schools and providing crucial machinery and patient financing. This reduces food imports, keeps money in the local economy, and creates hundreds of thousands of jobs along the agricultural value chain.
key_changes: Establishment of a Dedicated US$500 million Oil Palm Development Finance Window
Providing agriculture machinery for 50 agriculture districts with over 4,000 different machinery
Directing all schools, from basic to secondary, to purchase rice, maize, chicken and eggs produced in Ghana only

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: The Big Push Infrastructure Programme and Road Projects
topics.plain_summary: The government is deploying massive investments into physical infrastructure, specifically highlighting the addition of the Accra-Kumasi Expressway and the Adawso-Ekye Amanfrom Bridge, alongside a World Bank-funded program to build 1,000 kilometers of agricultural enclave roads.
topics.why_it_matters: For everyday travelers and farmers, these road networks drastically cut down travel time, reduce transport costs, and make it easier to get crops from farms to markets without heavy post-harvest losses. It stimulates local economies and creates tens of thousands of direct and indirect construction jobs.
key_changes: Adding the Accra-Kumasi Expressway and the Ekye Amanfrom-Adawso Bridge to the Big Push Infrastructure Programme
Implementing a three-year programme to construct 1,000 kilometers of agricultural enclave roads

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: Education Reforms: Ending Double-Track and Enhancing Basic Education
topics.plain_summary: The government is launching the Ghana Secondary Learning Improvement Programme (GSLIP) to entirely eliminate the double-track system in secondary schools, alongside wide-scale infrastructure and textbook provisions for basic education.
topics.why_it_matters: Parents and students benefit directly from the end of the crowded double-track school calendar, allowing children to attend school full-time in safe, modern environments. Improved basic school infrastructure and free textbooks ease financial burdens on families and elevate the overall quality of education.
key_changes: Rolling out the Ghana Secondary Learning Improvement Programme (GSLIP) to end the double-track system
Constructing 200 new Junior High Schools, 200 primary schools, 200 kindergartens, 400 teachers' bungalows, and 400 places of convenience
Providing free comprehensive curricula-based textbooks for learners

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: Health Sector Initiatives and MahamaCares
topics.plain_summary: The government is expanding healthcare infrastructure by building and completing regional and district hospitals, while leveraging the newly created Ghana Medical Trust Fund (MahamaCares) to finance treatments for non-communicable diseases.
topics.why_it_matters: For ordinary citizens, especially those suffering from chronic illnesses like cancer, diabetes, and kidney diseases, the MahamaCares fund removes the agonizing choice between paying for life-saving medical care and maintaining their livelihoods. Expanding hospitals also brings healthcare closer to underserved regions.
key_changes: Commencing construction of six new regional hospitals for newly created regions and two district hospitals at Bole and Shama
Completing ten abandoned Agenda 111 hospital projects
MahamaCares to introduce a comprehensive non-communicable disease (NCD) financing policy

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: Agriculture, Food Security, and Agro-Processing Allocations
topics.plain_summary: The government is investing heavily in agriculture to improve food security, lower food inflation, and support farmers through specific funding programs, infrastructure, and loans.
topics.why_it_matters: These agricultural investments help local farmers protect their harvests from going to waste, improve access to markets via better roads, and lower food prices for everyday families.
key_changes: We are providing GH¢245 million in 2026 to the Ministry of Food and Agriculture.
we are establishing a dedicated GH¢6.9 billion Oil Palm finance window to support the implementation of the National Policy on Integrated Oil Palm Development (2026–2032).
we have allocated GH¢828 million for the construction of 1,000km of agriculture enclave roads.
We have allocated GH¢690 million to commence the operationalization of the Farmer Service Centers.
We have allocated GH¢200 million to the Ghana Buffer Stock Company to purchase the glut in food produce and reduce the losses to our farmers.
We have allocated GH¢100 million for aquaculture development.

topics.title: Energy and Infrastructure Funding
topics.plain_summary: Significant funds are allocated to improve electricity access, settle energy sector debts, and build major roads and bridges to open up the country.
topics.why_it_matters: Reliable power and better roads make travel easier, cut transportation costs, reduce vehicle wear and tear, and keep businesses running without constant interruptions.
key_changes: We have allocated GH¢2.0 billion for Phase I of the Rural Electricity Acceleration and Urban Intensification Initiative in 2026.
We have also allocated an amount GH¢15.2 billion for energy sector shortfall payments.
We have allocated an amount of GH¢4.8 billion to pay legacy IPP debt in 2026.
we have allocated an amount of GH¢4.3 billion to the Ministry of Road and Highways for road construction.
we have allocated GH¢3.0 billion to the Ghana Road Maintenance Trust Fund to construct 10km each in 166 constituencies in 2026
we are allocating GH¢30.0 billion in 2026 for the Big Push Infrastructure Programme for strategic roads and bridges.

topics.title: Education Sector Support and School Programs
topics.plain_summary: The government is funding free secondary education, infrastructure repairs, learning materials, school feeding, and various allowances to support students and teachers.
topics.why_it_matters: Families will save money on school fees, registration costs, and supplies, while children benefit from better classrooms, free meals, and essential learning materials.
key_changes: we have allocated an amount of GH¢33.3 billion to the Ministry of Education for its programmes and activities in 2026.
an amount of GH¢9.9 billion has been allocated for the Ghana Education Trust Fund (GETFund).
we have provisioned an amount of GH¢4.2 billion for implementation of the Free Secondary Education in 2026.
we have allocated an amount of GH¢1.1 billion under the Ghana Secondary Learning Improvement Programme (GSLIP) in 2026.
The “No-Fee-Stress” policy will continue and we have allocated GH¢537 million in 2026.
We have allocated GH¢25 million for Free Tertiary Education for Persons with Disabilities.
We have allocated GH¢1.98 billion for the School Feeding Programme.
We have allocated GH¢292 million for free sanitary pads for girls.
We have also allocated GH¢207 million for Teacher Trainee Allowances.
Additionally, we have allocated GH¢169 million for BECE registration.

topics.title: Healthcare and Social Protection Programs
topics.plain_summary: Funding is directed toward health insurance claims, chronic disease care, hospital construction, nursing allowances, and poverty reduction programs like LEAP.
topics.why_it_matters: Ordinary people gain better access to affordable healthcare, medications, financial assistance for chronic conditions, and direct social support for low-income households.

topics.title: Economic Recovery and Budget Conclusion for 2026
topics.plain_summary: The government reported major economic improvements after taking office in January 2025, noting that inflation dropped to single digits, the Cedi appreciated against the US dollar, and public debt decreased. Programs like the 24-Hour Economy, the Big Push infrastructure project, and expanded social protections are moving forward to support growth and jobs.
topics.why_it_matters: Ordinary citizens and businesses face a more stable economic environment with single-digit inflation and a stronger Cedi, which helps lower the cost of living and import expenses. Expanded social programs and new job creation initiatives aim to ease everyday hardships and create long-term opportunities for families and workers across the country.
key_changes: GDP growth rose from 5.3 percent in 2024 to 6.3 percent in the first half of 2025.
Inflation dropped sharply from 23.8 percent at the end of December 2024 to single digits, 8 percent, by October 2025.
Ghana’s total public debt declined sharply from GH¢726.7 billion (61.8% of GDP) in December 2024 to GH¢630.2 billion (45.0% of GDP) by October 2025.
